title: Permissions
description: Who can read, change and run a file, and how to change that.

exercises.task: Make a file called hello.sh that holds the line: echo hello
exercises.hint: echo prints text and > sends it into a file: echo "some text" > <file>

exercises.task: Look at the permissions of hello.sh.
exercises.hint: ls -l <file> is the long listing. The first column, like -rw-r--r--, is three groups: you, your group, everyone else. r = read, w = change, x = run.

exercises.task: There's no x yet, so it can't be run. Make hello.sh runnable.
exercises.hint: chmod changes permissions, and +x adds 'can be run': chmod +x <file>
To run a program in this folder, put ./ in front of its name: ./<file>

exercises.task: Create an empty file called secret.txt.
Make secret.txt private: only you can read and change it.
exercises.hint: Permissions can be numbers: read is 4, change is 2, run is 1, added up for you, your group, everyone else. 600 = you read and change (4+2), nobody else anything: chmod 600 <file>

exercises.task: Check it worked: look at the permissions of secret.txt.
exercises.hint: ls -l <file>. You should see -rw------- : only the first group has letters.

exercises.task: Look at the permissions of the shared folder itself, not what's inside it.
exercises.hint: ls -l <folder> lists what's inside. Add d for the folder itself: ls -ld <folder>. On a folder, x means 'can go into it'.

done: You just read permissions with ls -l and ls -ld, and changed them with chmod +x and chmod 600.
